Dear Investor,
This week, we look at Europe’s economic outlook from resilient growth and persistent inflation to rising fiscal pressures and investment needs. We also examine whether Europe can fund its next growth cycle while managing higher debt, borrowing costs and refinancing risks.

Europe · Economy
Europe Is Growing, But Not Everyone Is Joining the Recovery
The euro area economy grew 0.4% in Q3, twice as fast as analysts expected, showing that Europe has remained more resilient despite high energy prices and financial market pressure. However, the chart clearly shows that growth remains highly uneven across major economies. Spain continues to outperform, supported by domestic demand, job creation and population growth, while Germany grew modestly, Italy stagnated and France contracted by 0.1%. The stronger euro area headline therefore does not necessarily mean that the region’s underlying growth momentum is equally strong everywhere.
Inflation Remains the Bigger Problem
Inflation remains well above the ECB’s 2% target across several major economies. Italy’s inflation accelerated to 5.6%, Spain remained at 4.9%, while France rose to 3.8%. This creates a difficult backdrop because the ECB cannot simply focus on weak growth when price pressures remain elevated across much of the region.
Energy Is Driving the Latest Inflation Shock
The broader inflation picture becomes clearer when looking at energy prices. After remaining relatively subdued through much of 2024 and 2025, Eurozone energy inflation has surged sharply in 2026, reaching 21% in October. This suggests that the latest rise in headline inflation is being driven primarily by the energy shock rather than a broad acceleration in underlying price pressures. This distinction is important for the ECB. Stable core inflation argues against aggressive tightening, but rapidly rising energy and food prices still push headline inflation further away from target and raise the risk of broader spillovers. Markets are therefore increasingly expecting another rate hike in December, leaving the ECB caught between controlling inflation and avoiding further pressure on Europe’s already fragile growth outlook.
Source: Morningstar
Europe’s Next Growth Story May Depend on Where It Invests
Europe’s challenge is not simply generating more growth, but directing capital into areas that can improve productivity and reduce strategic dependence. The biggest investment needs are emerging in energy infrastructure, defence, digital technology, AI, semiconductors and industrial modernisation. Europe has strong companies and technical capabilities, but high energy costs, fragmented capital markets and limited scale-up financing have made it difficult for promising businesses to grow into global leaders. This makes investment in infrastructure and technology increasingly important not just for growth, but also for Europe’s competitiveness and economic security.
The investment opportunity may lie in sectors receiving strong policy support and sustained capital spending, including defence, energy and grid infrastructure, industrial automation, semiconductors, AI and digital infrastructure. For investors, the focus should be on whether Europe can convert its savings into productive investment and support long-term growth in these strategic sectors.
Europe’s Private Capital Gap: The Missing Fuel for Growth
Source: Financial Times
The chart highlights one of Europe’s biggest structural challenges: its inability to provide enough private capital for innovative companies to scale. US venture capital investment has generally been around 0.5–1% of GDP, while major European economies remain far lower, often around 0.1% or less. This gap becomes particularly important as sectors such as AI, cloud computing, robotics and advanced technology require increasingly large amounts of capital to grow. Europe is now trying to address this through initiatives such as the €5 billion Scaleup Europe Fund and proposals to make it easier for companies to operate across the EU. But the challenge is not only raising capital, it is also preventing promising European companies from moving abroad to access funding and scale. For Europe’s next phase of growth, building a deeper private capital ecosystem could be just as important as increasing government spending on infrastructure and defence.
Fiscal Policy Is Supporting Growth, But Debt Is Becoming a Constraint
European governments face a difficult balancing act: they need to spend more on defence and infrastructure to support growth, while rising interest costs are already putting pressure on public finances. The European Commission projects the euro area fiscal deficit at 3.3% of GDP in 2026, rising to 3.5% in 2027, meaning governments may need to issue even more debt.
Source: Financial Times
This pressure is not evenly spread. France and Belgium face greater investor scrutiny due to high debt, weak growth and fiscal uncertainty, while Spain and Ireland are viewed more favourably. This widening gap between stronger and weaker borrowers is becoming an important trend in European bond markets. Also, as long-term borrowing costs remain elevated, European governments are increasingly relying on shorter-maturity debt to manage financing costs and reduce pressure on bond markets today. However, this creates a trade-off: more debt will need to be refinanced sooner, leaving government budgets more exposed if interest rates remain high. In other words, borrowing shorter may ease pressure today, but it could increase Europe’s refinancing risk and interest cost burden in the years ahead.
Why It Matters
Europe remains resilient, but high inflation, rising borrowing costs and weak fiscal positions are creating pressure. The key challenge is whether Europe can fund investment in growth sectors while managing its growing debt and private capital gap. For investors, the focus should be on sectors benefiting from this investment cycle and countries with stronger growth and fiscal positions.
